content.p: For three years Alex Murdaugh was known as a convicted double murderer. On 13 May 2026 the South Carolina Supreme Court took that label away. In a unanimous ruling it overturned his 2023 convictions for killing his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, and ordered a new trial. The murders are therefore once more an accusation that a jury has yet to decide, and Murdaugh, who has denied them since the day he reported finding the bodies, is presumed innocent of them.

The ruling did not open the prison door. Murdaugh, a disbarred personal injury lawyer, pleaded guilty to financial crimes in both federal and state court, and he is serving a 40-year federal sentence and a 27-year state sentence at the same time. NBC News noted that the ruling does not mean he will walk free. A judge has set the retrial to begin on 5 April 2027.
content.h2: The killings and the first trial
content.p: On 7 June 2021 Murdaugh phoned 911 a little after 10 p.m. to report that his wife Maggie, 52, and son Paul, 22, were dead outside the home at Moselle, the family's rural estate in Islandton. "My wife and child have been shot badly!" he told dispatchers, according to NPR's timeline. Two weapons were used, an assault-style rifle on Maggie and a shotgun on Paul, and the coroner put the deaths between 9 and 9:30 p.m. There were no eyewitnesses, and investigators never produced a murder weapon.

A grand jury in Colleton County indicted Murdaugh on two counts of murder and two weapons counts in July 2022, and he pleaded not guilty. His trial began on 23 January 2023 in Walterboro, in a courthouse NPR described as once a seat of power for the Murdaugh family; CNN reported that his father, grandfather and great-grandfather served as the local prosecutor, one after another, from 1920 to 2006.

Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his family to win sympathy and distract from financial crimes that were about to be exposed by his law firm, and from the fallout of a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the family of a teenager killed in a 2019 boat crash involving Paul. Much of the trial turned on a cellphone video Paul recorded at the family's dog kennels at about 8:45 p.m., minutes before investigators said the shootings happened. Witnesses identified Murdaugh's voice on it. He had told investigators he was not at the kennels, and when the video undid that account he took the stand and said, "I lied about being down there. And I'm so sorry that I did." He still denied the killings.

The jury deliberated for about three hours and convicted him on two counts of murder and two weapons counts on 2 March 2023. The next day Judge Clifton Newman sentenced him to two consecutive life terms. At sentencing Murdaugh said he would never hurt his wife or his son. Newman replied that it "might have been the monster you've become" when taking large numbers of opioid pills.

The murder case sat on top of a second scandal. In September 2021 Murdaugh was forced out of the law firm that carried his family's name, which later said he had taken millions of dollars from the firm and its clients. The next day he called 911 to say he had been shot in the head beside a road. State investigators said he had arranged the incident, with a gun supplied to another man, as an insurance fraud scheme that also involved assisted suicide. Murdaugh admitted the scheme nine days later and said it was meant to win his older son, Buster, a $10 million insurance payout.

He was arrested in October 2021, accused of diverting money from the estate of Gloria Satterfield, the family's longtime housekeeper, who died after a fall at Moselle in 2018. A court ordered him in 2022 to pay more than $4.3 million to her family. The South Carolina Supreme Court disbarred him in July 2022.

On 21 September 2023 he pleaded guilty in federal court to 22 counts: 14 of money laundering, five of wire fraud, one of bank fraud and two of conspiracy. He told the judge, "I want to take responsibility." The plea deal asked that any federal sentence run at the same time as his state sentence, and it required him to pay back about $9 million and to take a lie detector test if asked. In November 2023 Judge Newman gave him 27 years on the state financial charges, at a hearing where cheated clients were able to confront him.

On 1 April 2024 US District Judge Richard Gergel sentenced him to 40 years, ten more than the 30 years federal prosecutors had recommended, and ordered restitution of more than $8.7 million. Gergel cited the "staggering human toll" of the crimes and the way Murdaugh had targeted people who were injured, sick or grieving. He dismissed Murdaugh's claim that opioid addiction explained his conduct, saying "no truly impaired person could pull off the complexity of some of these transactions." Murdaugh told the court he was filled with sorrow and guilt. The sentence runs at the same time as the state term.

The appeal rested on Rebecca "Becky" Hill, the Colleton County clerk of court, who was assigned to oversee the evidence and the jury during the trial. Months after the verdict, Murdaugh's lawyers filed statements from jurors saying Hill had spoken to them about the case.

In January 2024 a hearing was held before retired Chief Justice Jean Toal, who was appointed to examine the allegations. One juror, identified only as Juror Z, said Hill told jurors to watch Murdaugh's actions and "watch him closely" when he testified. "She made it seem like he was already guilty," the juror said, though she also said that pressure from fellow jurors had done more to move her vote. The other 11 jurors said outside influence did not shape their verdicts, and one recalled hearing Hill say "watch his body language." Hill denied ever speaking to jurors about the case. Rhonda McElveen, the Barnwell County clerk, who helped at the trial, testified that Hill had spoken of writing a book "because she wanted a lake house," and that a guilty verdict would sell more copies.

Toal found that Hill was "not completely credible" and had been drawn by "the siren call of celebrity", but she refused a new trial. She ruled that the defence had to show Hill's remarks directly led jurors to change their minds, and said she would not overturn a verdict "on the strength of some fleeting and foolish comments by a publicity-seeking clerk of court."

Hill later faced her own legal consequences. According to NPR's timeline, on 8 December 2025 she pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice and perjury, over access to graphic photographs from the case and lying about it, and to two counts of misconduct in office. She was sentenced to probation and community service. NBC News reported her telling the court, "There is no excuse for the mistakes I made. I'm ashamed of them." CNN noted that she has never been charged with jury tampering.

The justices heard argument on 11 February 2026. Chief Justice Kittredge observed that some of Hill's statements, taken alone, "don't move the needle, arguably", but that together with her urging jurors not to be misled they "take on a very nefarious message." Prosecutors argued the guilty verdict did not come from Hill's behaviour and pointed to inconsistencies in the jurors' accounts.

On 13 May 2026 a 27-page opinion signed by all five justices (Kittredge, Few, James, Hill and Verdin) held that the court below had been wrong. Hill, they wrote, "egregiously attacked Murdaugh's credibility and his defense, thus triggering the presumption of prejudice," and had "placed her fingers on the scales of justice." They described her interference as accomplished outside the knowledge of the trial judge and the lawyers on both sides, and called her effort "breathtaking and disgraceful" and "unprecedented in South Carolina." The earlier finding that the judge's instructions had cured any problem failed, they said, because the disparaging remarks came from an officer of the court.

The court also raised a second concern. The trial judge, it said, went too far in letting jurors hear about Murdaugh's financial crimes, which the prosecution relied on as a motive. At the first trial Judge Newman had allowed it, reasoning that defence questions to witnesses about character and possible motive opened the door. Murdaugh's lawyers said evidence of the financial crimes "went far beyond what was necessary" and that on retrial "that will not be permitted."

The reactions split along predictable lines. Attorney General Alan Wilson said he "respectfully" disagreed and would "aggressively seek to retry" Murdaugh as soon as possible. The defence said Murdaugh had maintained from the start that he did not kill his wife and son. Eric Bland, a lawyer for some of the financial-crime victims, said his clients had "forgiven Alex, but they have not forgotten what he has done."

Murdaugh, then 58, appeared on 29 June 2026 at a hearing in Lexington County, shackled and in an orange jumpsuit. Judge Debra McCaslin, who said she knew nothing about the first trial, set the retrial to begin on 5 April 2027. "When I say April 5th, we're picking a jury and going forward," she said. Harpootlian objected to a jury seeing his client in chains when he has been convicted only of financial crimes; prosecutor Creighton Waters said restraints and jumpsuits are needed for security whenever an inmate is moved.

The defence filed motions seeking a change of venue, saying the 14th Circuit, which includes Colleton County, is where "the Murdaugh name has been synonymous with the local legal system for nearly a century". It also asked for independent DNA testing of material taken from under Maggie Murdaugh's left-hand fingernails, which the State Law Enforcement Division found came from an unknown and unrelated man. Prosecutors answered that the DNA was of "limited consequence" and that nothing showed a struggle, since she had no defensive wounds. Murdaugh's lawyers also sought a laptop in prison to review more than 20,000 pages of documents; the prison warden refused to allow one in his cell.

By the start of October 2026 the disputes had shifted to evidence. In a letter reported by WCBD on 2 October, Harpootlian told the judge that three motions to compel and five written discovery requests were unresolved, and that apart from DNA samples released after an August court order the state had produced nothing the defence had asked for since March 2023. Requests included raw crime-scene laser-scan data and cellphone extraction files. "The defense is at a standstill," he wrote. A status conference was scheduled for later in the month.

NPR and NBC both reported that even a new trial would not free him, because of the financial sentences. A jury will be asked a question the first one answered: whether he shot his wife and son. Until it does, the allegation remains unproven.
